extracted.intended_audience: data journalists and reporters (including non-technical journalists) who want to produce data-driven feature stories, especially those working with limited resources or without in-house developers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for producing feature-length journalism that integrates data visualisations — covering sourcing and cleaning data, choosing and building visualisations (static or interactive), laying out the story, and establishing repeatable workflows using accessible tools/platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the data you need
rubrics_metrics.description: At the heart of every data-driven feature story is (surprise, surprise) the data. Depending on your story, you might be sourcing data from government agencies, NGOs, academic researchers, or even private companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedicate time to sourcing exactly what you need. Many datasets require sleuthing — emails, phone calls, or formal FOIA (or equivalent) requests — so be patient. Much useful data is online but may not be in the format you need (beware the dreaded PDF).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean your data
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and clean source data; issues in source data will feed into your visualisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect data to arrive in closed formats (e.g., PDFs) or with impenetrable/inconsistent schemas; cleaning may be the most time-consuming part of the workflow. Manage issues as you go, and consider giving feedback to the data source (e.g., government agencies) to encourage better future releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide what to include (and what not to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose which datasets and elements to visualise — don’t include everything you have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data journalists must 'kill their darlings' and only include data that is critical to the feature story being told. Import your draft into the publishing platform early to think about how visualisations will work on-screen and to align content with platform features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualise your data appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Select visualisation methods and tools that match your skills, software, and budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options range from R/Python and BI tools like Tableau to open-source mapping tools such as QGIS. There are many tools for non-technical journalists; start small, don’t be intimidated, and don’t be afraid to make mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide between static and interactive outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether to publish static assets (images of charts/maps) or interactive/dynamic visualisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If developer resources are limited, use techniques that make static images feel dynamic (e.g., Scrollmation). If you have technical skill or resources, embed custom CSS, JavaScript, or HTML and use mapping libraries (Mapbox, Leaflet, OpenLayers) or interactive charts from other tools. Choose the approach that balances reader experience and maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay out your story with visualisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the story’s layout to integrate data visualisations effectively within the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mix of elements (title sections, scrollmation sections/backgrounds, reveal images, embedded media, GIFs, fully responsive images). Avoid overusing one visual feature (e.g., don’t overuse Scrollmation); mix media, think about image file formats, and ensure responsiveness (automated text-over-image formatting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise story and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A tool can build a beautiful package, but the story is the most important element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on compelling storytelling and use data visualisations to support and enhance the narrative rather than letting effects drive the piece. The page emphasizes repeatedly: 'story is everything.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Build sustainable workflows and reuse assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easier to create and publish future stories by finding efficiencies and reusing work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you have a feature under your belt, create custom templates and reusable components to reduce future time/costs. Sustainable data journalism requires efficiencies — avoid starting from scratch each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try and evaluate publishing platforms and tools before committing
rubrics_metrics.description: Test platforms and tools to ensure they meet your needs before full adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try a platform (e.g., Shorthand offers free accounts) to learn features and limits; upgrade only when ready to publish. Check platform-specific features (scrollytelling, Scrollmation, responsive behaviors) and prepare visualisations to take advantage of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from examples and industry standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Study exemplary data-driven feature stories to understand how data and narrative combine effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites examples (The Telegraph, Sky News, Guardian, Washington Post, ProPublica, La Nación, The Upshot, FiveThirtyEight) that demonstrate excellence in fundamentals: engaging storytelling supported by clear, compelling visualisations. Use these as models for design, sourcing, and narrative integration.
